newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-AS LONG AS MONEY ROLLS IN TYSON WANTS MORE CHILDREN.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-AS LONG AS MONEY ROLLS IN TYSON WANTS MORE CHILDREN.

text.p: As long as former heavyweight champion Mike Tyson continues to generate $30 million paydays, he plans to continue producing offspring.
"Every time I see that situation going well with more fights and good purses, I'll have another child then," said Tyson, whose wife Monica is pregnant with their second.
Tyson also has a child from a previous relationship and treats Monica's seven-year-old daughter as one of his own.

He and reigning heavyweight champion Evander Holyfield are each expected to earn around $30 million for Saturday's big rematch. And Tyson seems keenly aware these days that each challenge in the ring translates into a more lucrative future for his children.
"Every fight is a different future for my children. I base my life for my financial gain," Tyson said Monday night as he held court for reporters at promoter Don King's posh home outside Las Vegas.
"We have to take care of our children and I'm just looking forward to that," the one-time world's most feared fighter turned proud papa continued. "This is life and we have a life beyond boxing.
"I'm glad I'm at a stage in my life where I have children. A few years from now I won't be in this business and I can pay greater attention to them."
Tyson then smiled and added: "I love them, but I love me."
The former champion, who two weeks ago was predicting a sensational victory over Holyfield in their rematch, was in more of of a philosophical mood as he reflected upon his loss last November.

"I can't get caught up about some defeat because that's life, building, persevering and coming back from the loss," said Tyson, who insisted his defeat to Holyfield was more personally shocking to him than his stunning upset by Buster Douglas in 1990.
"The easiest way in the world to fail is trying to please everybody," added Tyson.
"You are who you are and that's just the way you are. We live, we play, we die hard. That's just the way it is, man."
About again facing Holyfield, who stopped Tyson in the 11th round to hand him just his second loss in 47 professional fights, Tyson said: "I don't know if it's a turning point for my career.
"I'm not dealing with a middle-age crisis or anything," joked Tyson, who turns 31 next week.
Although the Tyson camp did its best to stir up animosity between their fighter and Holyfield before the first bout, Tyson said there were no ill feelings between them.

"Cus D'Amato was a great emotional teacher and we learned from him to never take anything personally as far as the job is concerned," he said, summoning the name of his revered mentor and the trainer who set him on the path to becoming the world's youngest heavyweight champion.
"I always don't try to get personal. I just fight," he said.

Then perhaps remembering that the purpose of the media gathering was to generate interest in the Holyfield rematch and increase pay-per-view revenue Tyson said: "This is a very big fight. It's probably the biggest fight ever.
"It will be a great feeling to win the title back, but it will only mean something when I grasp it."
